item.name: 7 Wonders
item.comment:
4-5 (6, 3, 7) (open)
6.5: Rating based on only one game, need to play again. Duel feels like a much better version of 7 Wonders though.
Update: Played another game at 6. Ok, I can see where this game has a spot - it's one of very few strategy games that can be played in a relatively short time with 6 or 7 people. But, it still feels very multiplayer solitaire, luck has a huge factor, not that engaging. Keeping the rating at 6.5. But for a better game that plays well with 6 in a similar time, and is way more fun and interactive, I would recommend Medici.

item.name: 7 Wonders Duel
item.comment:
2 (open)
One of the best two-player games. Not too long, nor too short. Great direct player interaction. Luck may play some role.

item.name: Air, Land, & Sea: Spies, Lies, & Supplies
item.comment:
(open)
One play. Achieves an interesting game with very few cards, but also because of that, leaves options to brute-force compute the ending, which slows it down.

item.name: Alchemists
item.comment:
4 (3) (open)
Nice, great idea, but feels too long for what it is. The deduction aspect is a bit easy, but still adds a non-traditional aspect to a worker-placement game.

item.name: Architects of the West Kingdom
item.comment:
(shrink)
First play evaluation: Quick turns, fun moments and overall feel-good vibes. Enough interaction, albeit it lacks a deeper shared state that players can modify to affect the game more broadly. More tactical than deeply strategic. A great option for a faster game for 5. Would definitely seek to play again.

item.name: Ark Nova
item.comment:
(shrink)
One play only. Cards are interesting and the whole game brings good feelings, but it does feel in most aspects as multiplayer solitaire, interaction is low, everyone chasing and building their own thing. Between this and Terraforming Mars, I think I prefer TM, but I gotta play this some more.

item.name: Azul
item.comment:
2-4 (open)
Easy rules, quick setup and tear-down, neither too short, nor too long, amazingly tactile. But has some pretty deep strategy and betting on how opponents would play. Also allows some mean play sometimes. Though I generally prefer some more player interaction and "tightness".

item.name: Babylonia
item.comment:
(open)
It's a good game, and I feel with more games with the same group, deep play will emerge, but unfortunately, for some reason, it flops with most people I try it with - it's just not sufficiently exciting in the first play, so it's hard to convince people to play it over other games.
I have had much more success with family and friends with the other Knizia tile-laying games we've played - Yellow & Yangtze and Blue Lagoon. I think that Babylonia has much more growing potential than Blue Lagoon, but Blue Lagoon feels somewhat more interactive, while with a more chill vibe with its Polynesian art. Y&Y feels both deeper and more interactive than both.
Edit: Bumping up, this is growing both on me and on people I play with.
Edit: This has become a favorite of mine and the group. Game is quick, interactive and strategic.

item.name: Barrage
item.comment:
4 (3) (open)
Tight, thinky and very thematic. Great player interaction. It's complex to play strong, but because rules make perfect sense with the theme, it's actually easy to teach, grasp and play correctly.
It's a long game though. Also individual turns can turn long.

item.name: Beyond the Sun
item.comment:
3 (4,2) (open)
Very solid. Clean and fairly simple rules, plays quickly - 2h for 3 players is right, great visual design (IMHO) which favors readability over flashiness. The tech tree works well to specialize the players differently, and is filled with humor and interesting tidbits (e.g. cards like the Museum of Retired Spacecraft).
What it lacks are maybe some bigger "Wow!" moments.

item.name: Biblios
item.comment:
3 (4,2) (open)
A great bidding game, that's supposed to be a filler but actually has depth. Simple rules, yet proper play is very non-obvious.

item.name: Blue Lagoon
item.comment:
4 (3) (open)
Wy wife and daughter love this one a lot, the theme helps there. My wife usually dislikes boardgames and this one is one of the few she would actually play.
Theme and art-wise it feels like a family game, but in reality it's quite interactive and cutthroat - it's a tight competition and there is even the opportunity for some nasty play here and there.
Pros: - Turns are super short, it's just a single "place one token somewhere". Hence it plays very breezy. Still, the decision space is sufficiently non-trivial. - Rules are also simple, I have no issue recalling them and teaching others after not having played for some time. - Setup and tear-down are very quick - Plays well at all player counts
Con: - It's a nice puzzle, but at the end it does not feel too deep. I feel it will reach a plateau for us after not too many games.
Overall, very recommended.

item.name: Brass: Birmingham
item.comment:
(open)
Interesting, beautiful and thematic. This is one of the games that best model economy. The feeling of supply and demand is very real. High levels of interaction.
Setup and tear-down are pretty nasty. It could also get a bit fiddly at moments, e.g. players looking for what they actually can do. As a result, it usually runs longer than one plans.
Edit: After having played it 10+ times, I do think I like the mood of Birmingham a little bit more than Lancashire. Overall both versions are some of the very best games out there. Raising rating to 10.

item.name: Brass: Lancashire
item.comment:
4 (3) (open)
Need to play more to rate and compare to Birmingham.
Edit: After several plays - can't pick between this one and Birmingham, but both are great and feel different enough to be worth playing both.
Lancashire is tighter and players might feel blocked at times, it is probably a tad more cut-throat. Birmingham is a bit more open.
Read the rest of my comments on Birmingham.

item.name: Brian Boru: High King of Ireland
Broom Service
item.comment:
(open)
Positive impression from first game. It does feel random, but I can see that there are options for deeper strategies there with more plays. It seems there is sufficient information available to be able to mitigate the randomness over the course of a game. It also seems there are options to use different strategies.
Theme and art are both great. Length is also adequate. Lots of interaction, lots of fun moments.

item.name: Bus
item.comment:
(open)
Simple, tight, fun and interactive, but I prefer both Food Chain Magnate and The Great Zimbabwe from Splotter.

item.name: Carcassonne Big Box 6
item.comment:
2-4 (open)
The base game is fine, but not my favorite. The rating is for the base game, plus the 1-2 essential things from the expansions (e.g. the big workers).
The Big Box is unnecessary and way too big. I do not recommend buying it, unless you're some huge fan of the game. Most expansions in it are "Meh, whatever".

item.name: The Castles of Burgundy
item.comment:
2 (3) (shrink)
Played only on BGA for now. It's satisfying and feel good, but very solitaire and I can't see a ton of depth in it. Maybe with more plays? We'll see... Would play, but usually I seek more interactive, cut-throat economic interaction on a common board, not this heads-down action-optimizing puzzle.

item.name: Catan
item.comment:
4 (3) (open)
It's a classic for a reason. This was my gateway into boardgaming, for a long time it was the only boardgame we had at home (apart from cards, chess, etc.), and I've played countless games.
Good player interaction. Mechanics tie well with the theme. Has strategic decisions. Trading allows "playing the players", not only the game. Some fun surprise moments, but not too often. Dice luck plays a huge role, probably a bit too much, but often that sort of luck factor and thrill is what players seek. But when the dice are against you for several turns in a row, it could get annoying, and there is no mechanism to compensate.
Has a bit of a runaway leader problem sometimes. Also if a player gets blocked on the map, they may have a very miserable game. One of the annoying aspects is that on some turns you simply cannot do anything.

item.name: Chess
item.comment:
2 (open)
It's such a classic for a reason. Simply a beautiful game. Utter simplicity in rules, yet so often one ends up in a uniquely-feeling game. Amazing "Wow!" moments. I'm not a super strong player and don't play too often, but one cannot help but appreciate the genius design and balance of the game. One of the very few games where I'd gladly enjoy watching others play.
Also, with the proper wooden pieces, chess beats almost any other game in terms of beauty and tactility.

item.name: Citadels
item.comment: 5-6 (4) (open) Played a long time ago. It was... fine. But haven't had a desire to play again. Perhaps too light for my taste, while still being not to short.

item.name: Codenames: Pictures
item.comment:
6,8,4 (open)
Nice and simple, works with kids. But the downtime while the "storyteller" thinks is a huge downside.
As a whole, for a similar kind of game, I much prefer Decrypto. But Codenames plays faster, which is often important for party games.

item.name: Colt Express
item.comment:
5-6 (4) (open)
It can be fun the first 2-3 times, then it loses its appeal. Too random, no strategy, too much of a "party" game for my liking.
But my rating would have been significantly higher if this was not designed as a full-blown big box game. This could have been a deck of cards, then it would make much more sense. The cardboard wagons are a simply unnecessary use of space.

item.name: Concordia Venus
item.comment:
4 (3) (open)
Only two plays so far.
Greatest asset is that rules are really elegant. Turns are also short enough, so downtime is not bad. It's overall a nice, feel-good theme, vibes are positive, without the game being just a shower of points and resources everywhere, there is enough tightness in the resources.
Biggest downside is that overall it's a bit flat, you don't have big ways to impact the common state or your opponents, the interaction is mostly some competing for positioning or cards, but without full blocking. It's not too little, but not super impactful either. There aren't some nice "Wow" moments.
And also, being a point salad, it does lack a bit of "tension".
Concordia is often given as an example for a good next step up from Catan, I disagree, Catan overall has more interesting things going for it, and more opportunities for playing the players, not just the game. Hence I also rate it higher, despite it also having bigger "defects".

item.name: Conspiracy: Abyss Universe
item.comment:
2-4 (open)
Pretty nice little filler game. Plays fast and for this time, it offers a decent level of depth.

item.name: The Crew: The Quest for Planet Nine
item.comment:
4 (3) (open)
Good, but it feels similar to, and I like that one better, to the classic trick-taking card game "Oh, Hell". I am also not a huge fan of the cooperative nature of The Crew.

item.name: Cuzco
item.comment:
(open)
One play, somewhat long for what it is. Amazing table presence. The festivals feel somewhat tacked on and unnecessary. Still a solid game I would play again.

item.name: Decrypto
item.comment:
6,4 (8) (open)
My most favorite variant of "word/associations game" out there. Meta-game starts building as the rounds progress, listening to other team's discussions can be super fun. Works with adults, works with small kids. I think 6 players work better than 4 exactly because with 6 there are open discussions on the table. There is no downtime - no matter whose turn it is to provide clues, everyone on the table can be thinking.
It could be a longer game though than most other similar games (e.g. Codenames).
It does require the right group to be really fun, but when it's fun it's really fun.

item.name: Dixit
item.comment:
6,5 (4) (open)
A classic in the "how do others think" genre, along with Codenames.
But it's a bit too much an activity more than a game for me.
In this genre, my firm recommendation is Decrypto, the growing meta over the course of the game there elevates it a lot.

item.name: Dominion
item.comment:
3 (2,4) (open)
Not a fan. Maybe I'm overall not a huge fan of deck-building, cause I find it a nuisance in other games too. But the total lack of connection between theme and mechanics in Dominion is what kills it completely for me.

item.name: Dune: Imperium
item.comment:
(open)
Only two plays. It feels it could grow on me, but I need more plays. But it's quite long. 8 for now.
Edit: Two more plays at 3 and 4. Excellent tension, mental play, exciting twists, regular "Wow!" moments. Raising to 9. Final outcome can be a bit too dependent on luck.
Edit 2: More games. Luck seems to play a bit too big of a role. Some factions seem underpowered.
For now, I like this version better than Uprising - the spies in Uprising expand the space of possible moves a lot there, which slows turns down, also the worms feel like they dictate and force the game into particular paths too much.

item.name: Dune: Imperium – Uprising
item.comment:
(open)
One play only, but for now I'd rate this lower than the original Dune:I. It felt a bit too swingy, and ended a bit too fast. Also agents seem to kill some of the elegance/simplicity of the game. Cards were more interesting overall though. Need to play more to see how my opinion will evolve.

item.name: Five Tribes: The Djinns of Naqala
Food Chain Magnate
item.comment:
3-4 (open)
Very interactive and the economy feels very real. Mechanics-wise, it's pretty genius. I like the art too, no issue with its style or simplicity - it makes the board quick to read.
But it could go painfully long. And the lack of a catch-up mechanism could totally discourage a player from playing again.
Edit: After multiple plays, the design is simply amazing. Simple and intuitive rules, games turn vastly different, level of interaction is unparalleled. Raising rating to 10.

item.name: Gaia Project
item.comment:
3-4 (2) (open)
Only two plays at 2p. The potential is visible, but I need to play more, and with more people.
Turns can get very combo-ish and this makes the game feel a bit slow sometimes. It's also quite long.

item.name: Galaxy Trucker (Second Edition)
item.comment:
3-4 (open)
Not a huge fan of frantic realtime mechanics in games. Up a notch for the humour in the book. And it's overall a funny premise. Randomness galore.

item.name: The Gallerist
item.comment:
(open)
After one play, I liked this better than Kanban EV. Seemed more interactive and much less of a point salad. Still I'm not sure Lacerda is exactly my type of designer. Every action has implications on what it gives you now, what it gives you long term, what it gives you for the end game scoring, what action it gives one of your opponents, can they benefit too much from it, how it changes the board, etc... It's interesting, but it feels like a lot of your actions have purely coincidental side effects. And somehow your way of achieving your goals is never direct, it's by using the side effects of what you do. Compare this to a Splotter game where everyone has freedom to pick their strategy entirely directly, without limitations and without a myriad of hard-to-estimate and hard-to-control side effects.
Edit: After three plays, not sure I'd play more, reducing rating to 6.5. It's better at 4 players than 3. In any case, too many things are chance dependent, while quite important and impactful. E.g. whether another player would kick you out is essential sometimes, and many times pure luck. Not being able to repeat your action unless someone kicks you out is a random, illogical, non-thematic, game-killing limitation - it's actively taking away player agency. The point salad-ness is quite brutal.

item.name: Gloomhaven: Jaws of the Lion
item.comment:
2 (3,4) (open)
We started on this with my son and couldn't even pass the tutorial. I guess dungeon crawlers are not our thing. As a whole it felt super mechanical and... "procedural". Or maybe it's the cooperative nature of it that bothers me.
If we give it another go, I'll update the rating.
Update: Lowering to 4. As time passes, I have less and less desire to revisit. I think I generally dislike games like this with dice/card battling, character development, health stats, etc. I also dislike cooperative games. Basically this hits all the wrong chords for me.
Probably not the game's fault - the rating reflects my own subjective desire to play it, not that I think it's a fundamentally bad game (as is the case with other low ratings I've given).

item.name: El Grande
item.comment:
5 (4) (open)
Simple rules, not fiddly, not too long. I'm not a huge fan of area control / area majority overall, but here it seems to work better than other games in the genre I've tried (e.g. Root, Oath).

item.name: Great Western Trail
item.comment:
3 (4,2) (open)
It's an interesting game, that can also feel quite thematic. Also a pretty decent use of deck-building, a mechanism I'm not usually a fan of. But damn, the setup is so fiddly than I usually pass and pick something else just because of it. Also, it's longer than it feels it should be.

item.name: The Great Zimbabwe
item.comment:
(open)
After two plays at 3 and 5 players, TGZ shoots straight to my favorites. Super interactive and dynamic, very fun, cool theme, great art.
Only downside is that at 5p the board gets busy, the logistics start becoming quite difficult to track, and we had to reverse some moves due to bad calculations.
Second Splotter game I've played after Food Chain Magnate - they seem to be super skilled at nailing the aspects around common markets, economics and logistics, supply & demand, shared board and resources. Can't decide which one I like better... Now impatient to play their other games.
Edit: Ok, so after one more play at 3p - the ending can be mind-crushingly mathy. It's a full information game, which means that the last 2 moves could be min-maxed. It's difficult but doable, and in our last game, everyone had a shot at victory, so turns took long. It was interesting to play out various scenarios, but I feel a very very slight random element towards the end could have been useful to prevent min-maxing.

item.name: Hansa Teutonica: Big Box
item.comment:
5 (4) (open)
7.5 after two plays at 5 players. I like this, but don't love it. Moves are fast, and the game is simple conceptually. Interesting interactions.
But it's a bit hard for me to form a cohesive plan - other players' actions can move the state quite a lot. So it feels like it's more tactical/reactive than strategic. Maybe the strategic aspects will reveal with experience.
It's purely mechanical. The theme is totally disconnected from the mechanics, more so than most euros. It's pretty much impossible to think in more thematic terms than "cubes / discs / spaces".
The graphic design could be better - it's a bit hard to parse some aspects of the board state, e.g. cities are not sufficiently easily distinguishable from route positions.
Still, overall, this feels like one of the few games that has some depth to it, yet plays quick for 5 players and others' players turns are at least to some extent interesting to you. Overall it's a fun, enjoyable experience, but I haven't experienced true "Wow!" moments. Would gladly play again.

item.name: Harmonies
item.comment:
(shrink)
Played only on BGA, not in person. Very pleasant, but does not seem too deep. Shares some ideas with Azul, but Azul feels way more interactive. Here the game feels mostly multiplayer solitaire, with the occasional "meddling" with your opponent by taking whichever card or tokens suit them best. Still, it's a fun little puzzle, nice art, plays quick.

item.name: Hegemony: Lead Your Class to Victory
item.comment:
(shrink)
First play.
Interesting game. First time I see an asymmetric game that I like - the players are still playing the same "common" game and even if everyone plays differently, there is logical interaction and a logical common state. Everyone's goals and motivations seem thematic, not "made up" like in games like, say, Root. There is a lot of interaction and push/pull tension between the players. Temporary alliances form and dissolve often.
However, it was really long, 6+ hours with four players. Also, I feel that my strategy was too "dictated by the game", it felt like my decisions are mostly around "which action or card works tactically best right now" rather than real decisions with big impact on the game. I played as the Capitalists and won by 2 points, but there were no surprising "Wow" moves by anyone and I cannot point to any move and say "Yeah, this move was decisive for the game".
Maybe strategies will open up with further plays, and after I try the other classes.

item.name: High Frontier 4 All
item.comment:
(open)
Very hard to rate, but the TLDR is - nice interesting simulation, but sucks as a game and, as a game, definitely not worth the time.
As a multiplayer game, it kinda sucks: It's too convoluted, lacks smoothness, turns need too much back-tracking and computation, auctions + negotiations lack guiderails and can derail the turns, game starts way too slow (the first ~10-12 turns are used just collecting cards, trying to get some viable combination, this takes hours), interaction on the board is minimal, so it's a fairly heads-down experience. Some faction abilities and individual cards are impossible to understand, and googling does not yield enough results. Also, for a game of this complexity, the random element is huge...
There are also strange loopholes in the rules - for example the faction that removes the limit of 4 cards to participate in bids, combined with the rules around negotiating the transfer of cards, seems to break the game, allowing the negotiating players to bid very very high, bypassing the other players.
As a simulation, it may be considered interesting, exploring the map is some sort of fun activity. There is realism and a bit of humor. There are the occasional laughs and exciting moments, that's good.
For 1-2 players, it kinda works without being forbiddingly long (but it's still VERY slow and long). I expected that playing with 4 would make for a more interesting experience, and there really was _some_ interaction around bidding, which made things seemingly better, but it took us forever to fly even the first rocket, it moves way too slow. And the interaction just around bidding and the occasional negotiation was too little considering the vast beautiful map in front of us. Had some fun, but at the end, we cancelled the game at around the 6-7 hours mark, with two out of four solar cycles remaining.
Ultimately, if I'm gonna play a game this long and complex, I'd much rather play some gem of a game that puts guardrails so that players end up interacting in meaningful ways like one of Splotter's titles, Brass, Barrage, etc.

item.name: High Society
item.comment:
(open)
Just pure, interactive fun.
Played for first time, 4 times in a row with 5 players. Instant favorite. Plays fast, lots of fun, inspires great table talk, even some role playing. Lots of fun "wow" moments. Still thinky and requires both planning and some psychology. Games played differently due to different order in which cards were opened, it seems the game will offer enough variety. Osprey's edition has great art in Art Nouveau style that fits the game so well.
Knizia's bidding games are simply amazing. It's difficult for me to say which one I like best between Ra, Medici and High Society - all are great!

item.name: Iberian Gauge
item.comment:
(open)
Initial rating 7.5, upping to 8 after second play with five players.
Interactive, simple rules, plays fast enough, fun. Inspires great table talk and "playing the players". Shared incentives can mean there is very little to separate the players at times. If someone gets behind, the game might suck for them, they might not be able to get back into the game.
Overall, I consider this one a great option for a not-too-long-yet-still-strategic game for 5 players - there are not many games that fit this bill.

item.name: Imperial Settlers: Empires of the North
Imperium: Classics
item.comment:
1-2 (open)
Only one play till now that felt quite "Meh". I doubt this will grow on me.

item.name: Ingenious 3D
item.comment: This competes with Azul for me and I find it a bit better as a game, though component-wise Azul is miles ahead. Abstract game, simple rules, quick engaging play, high interaction, typical Knizia. Family loves it.

item.name: Innovation
item.comment:
(open)
We love this game and have played it probably 100+ times. It's just 105 cards, yet so often the game or situation we end up in feels unique. Way bigger variability than almost anything else we've played. Extremely fun moments sometimes. Highly interactive, in a great way. The progress of civilization as game progresses is very tangible - I am yet to find another game that's as good at this. Most games manage to create a unique story. Some situations that arise from time are little wonders on their own. Lots of surprising and funny moments.
Not too long, not too short. And for the length you feel you've played a more "epic" game than most others. Also probably the best "game size to amount of game" ratio of any game out there.
Plays great with 3. With 4, it's more random and maybe goes a bit too quick, but still offers a lot of fun. With 2 it can be a mean battle of wits. With four experienced players, playing with teams (2 vs. 2) is great.
It's very swingy, and way more tactical than strategic, there is quite a lot of luck. A player who seems to be losing can sometimes take the lead or win by pure chance. This often contributes to the fun, but can annoy some players. But most often better play still wins.
Some games may feel "Meh" or end too quickly with a runaway leader, but games are short enough that when this happens, you just go for another round.

item.name: Innovation Ultimate
item.comment:
(open)

item.name: Just One
item.comment:
6-7 (5) (open)
Decent variant of "associations", plays quick. The markers are a nuisance cause they dry up. But there are similar activities based on "associations" that don't require any materials.

item.name: Kanban EV
item.comment:
3 (4) (open)
Only one play, at 2p. Cannot say I saw the reasons for the praise, but will not rate until I have played several times with 3/4.
Edit: Second play at 3p.
Rules are complex, but once you start, the game actually flows fairly easily. Turns are quick. The worker placement mechanic plus the interaction with Sandra are great - there is a good level of interaction between players around it, turn order matters a lot, and players control it - which I like a lot.
People praise the theme to mechanics connection, I'm not so sold on this. The parts around working in a factory, getting rated, boasting about your own achievements - yes, those make sense, but the parts around cars, car parts, upgrading designs, tested designs, etc. - I'm failing to see the connection to the real world. All those concepts actually make understanding the rules more complex. An example for a euro game that feels much more tightly linked to the "real world", and as a result easier to grasp, is Barrage.
I am also not a fan of the point-salady nature of it. I wonder if it could have been avoided, e.g. if there was some "winner takes the prize" from each meeting, so that there was more tension between the meetings, and it felt as a tennis match where points and games matter, but at the end, the sets count.
Still, overall, it was an interesting game and I'd seek to play it again, but I'm not yet convinced this would grow on me to the level of praise the ratings here indicate. It feels production is carrying a lot of the weight for the current ratings.

item.name: The King Is Dead: Second Edition
item.comment:
3 (open)
Simple rules, super elegant, and really solid and thinky. Creates nice "Wow" moments sometimes. Downside is that maybe the beginning of the game feels too "unguided" and random - you play until some state develops, and only then your actions start becoming sufficiently informed. Maybe that's lack of experience though.

item.name: King of Tokyo
item.comment:
4-5 (6,3) (open)
Cannot understand the praise and popularity. Some pretty mindless dice-chucking and direct "I hit you, you hit me" type of thing. I'd probably give it a second chance if someone insists, but I wouldn't offer myself.

item.name: Kutná Hora: The City of Silver
Little Town
item.comment:
3-4 (2) (open)
Underrated game. It's quite interactive and even somewhat tight with the common map that players build together. The selection of available buildings means that every time, the "right" point-generating engines are different, which offers nice variability. There are both strategic and tactical decisions. It plays quick - in 45-60 minutes, but offers the feeling of a longer game. Package is small and component quality is nice.
Maybe it could have benefited from some variable turn order mechanic.
Perhaps the fact it's packaged in a "kids game" format hurts it.

item.name: The Lord of the Rings: Duel for Middle-earth
item.comment:
(open)
Super solid two-player game, one of the best, highly recommended. Not too long, nor too short. Great direct player interaction. Luck may play a big role.
Compared to 7 Wonders Duel, this seems to lead to even more tension and tighter games, so for now rating a bit higher, but let's see how it grows.
The added area control element is quite interesting. I am not so sure about the flat "1 coin per missing resource" change - it streamlines the game, sure, but the previous approach of "2 + how many opponent has" allowed for some clever nasty economic pressure on the opponent.

item.name: Lost Cities
item.comment:
(shrink)
Several quick plays on BGA. Quick enjoyable filler, plays very smooth. Not sure how deep it will be though. There is definitely some non-trivial luck of the draw element. In some ways reminds me of Mandala, which is of comparable length and complexity.

item.name: Lost Ruins of Arnak
item.comment:
3 (2,4) (shrink)
Feel good and nice theme, art is decent too (not my favorite style, but this is personal preference). But it's points everywhere, going up tracks, the connection between theme and mechanics is kinda loose, and level of interaction is not great.
It's often compared to Dune: Imperium due to mechanics, but they don't feel similar at all - Dune is a high-interaction, high-tension race, this here is a "walk in the park"...
Not a bad game, would definitely play again, but nothing amazing either.

item.name: Love Letter
item.comment:
4 (5,3,6) (open)
It's a very solid party filler that works great with kids. Plays fast, has fun moments. No deep strategy aspects. Scales well, I've had fun games at all player counts, including 2.
Still, if I have the chance, I'd much rather play something deeper.

item.name: Magic Maze
item.comment:
4 (5,3) (open)
I hated the realtime and "no talking" aspects of this. Also, the game felt like you are constantly searching for something. As though I've lost my keys... I'll have to be in a special mood to be convinced to play again.

item.name: Mandala
item.comment:
2 (open)
Very solid abstract two-player game. Quick setup, easy rules, deep strategy. Games go in 15-20 min, which is great. Contents fits in a small bag, so it's easy to carry around.
Perhaps it will lack the long-term variability appeal of deeper games like Chess, though. We'll see.

item.name: Master of Orion: The Board Game
Medici
item.comment:
(open)
One of the most well received games I've had on the first play. Played two times in a row, at 6p and 5p. All the excellent properties of a Knizia game - super simple rules, turns are relatively short, the whole game plays in a about 60-80 min, while the decisions are crunchy, table talk is active and there are lots of exciting moments. There is an element of luck, but it is well-manageable.
Let's see how it grows on me.

item.name: Mind MGMT: The Psychic Espionage “Game.”
item.comment:
3,2,5 (open)
Feels more hyped than it's worth it. The deduction is the very typical "brute-force through all possibilities" type. Yes, "Letters from Whitechapel" is longer, but it feels so much more thematic and pulls you into the world way more. The deduction there is also more interesting, there's some betting, there's looking for reactions, etc.

item.name: Minos: Dawn of the Bronze Age
Oath
item.comment:
4 (3,5) (open)
Probably liked this a tad better than Root, but it still suffers from the typical problem I see in many "area control" games. From some point onward, your turn is mostly making sure the next player won't win on their turn, and it goes like this for a loooong painful time.
Lots of king-making, and I disagree with all the reviews that try to state how great it is in this game, because of how it builds the story, blah-blah...
What I find nice are the interesting cards - there is richness there, thematically, in terms of art, and in variance.
This, the art, and the world-building, are what tickles my senses enough to want to play it 1-2 more times, but unless I see more interesting plays from them, I cannot rate better.

item.name: On Mars
item.comment: (open) One play. Convoluted, point-salad type of thing. Not a huge desire to play it again.

item.name: One Night Ultimate Werewolf
item.comment:
7,6,8 (5,9,10) (open)
If I have to play a party game, and we have the necessary number of people, this one is a great choice. Some games go "Meh", but very often some gem of a game happens.

item.name: One Night Ultimate Werewolf: Daybreak
item.comment:
6-8 (5,9,10) (open)
Have only played a couple of games, but I felt the roles are unnecessarily more complex than in the main game, and overall afterwards never felt the need to play and teach this variant than the more popular main game.
Additionally, probably because I didn't buy the main game and the expansion together, the card backs have a slightly different yellow tint. So playing both together unsleeved is not an option cause I know which card is from which set. I haven't bothered to sleeve.

item.name: Ora et Labora
item.comment:
(open)
One play at 3p, short game. Nice. Mostly short turns, interesting resource conversion, a decent amount of player interaction, feel-good theme, nice art. Some engine building but not sure how much the engine can be exploited outside of the moment you build the building - it seems that with the limited number of actions, building new buildings and preparing resources for settlement might be more important than running your engine.
The only other "big" Uwe game I've played is Caverna, and I think I liked Ora et Labora better (though Caverna was 2p which I don't consider an optimal count).

item.name: Orléans
item.comment:
4,3 (2) (open)
There are fun moments, but it's a point salad with interaction on the lower side - even with the expansion deeds board - and it seems to run longer than ideal for the fairly low depth and complexity.

item.name: Pan Am
item.comment:
(open)
Fairly light, a bit too much luck of the draw, but overall pretty enjoyable. Art is nice and the game has enough going to be able to recreate the "mood of the times".
It's a good option for playing with people who are new to boardgames. After a couple of games it feels replayability will not be great, the overall arc felt too similar. But for now I'd still gladly play if I'm in the mood for something lighter with a feel-good vibe.
Overall I'd probably recommend Ticket to ride over this for a similarly-themed lighter game that is good for beginners - it seems to offer more player agency and options to mitigate the luck, and more replayability.

item.name: Pandemic
item.comment:
4 (3,2) (open)
It's thematic and the mechanics tie well to the theme. Plays well with kids.
But it seems I'm not a huge fan of cooperative games. Also, it does feel a bit samey after 7-8 plays.

item.name: Patchwork
item.comment:
(open)
Solid, thinky and non-trivial puzzle. Took me several plays till my first victory, which is a good sign towards the depth of the game.

item.name: Port Royal
item.comment:
4,3 (5) (open)
Plays quick, fairly fun, offers some amount of strategic options, has some "wow" moments when some big risk turns OK, works well with kids. But it turns samey after several plays.

item.name: Power Grid
item.comment:
(open)
Great bidding game. The economic aspect with the market is also very strong. Supply and demand feel real. High levels of player interaction with the bidding, the map, the market.
It is on the long side, especially with more people, but I feel it's been worth it.
Gameplay feels smooth, not too many edge cases.
One downside I see is that the catch-up mechanic is probably too strong, to an extent that whatever players do, up until the last houses, everyone moves in a pack, which means the game is decided almost entirely in the last couple of rounds.
Have had great plays at 4 and 6, haven't tried 5, with 3 it didn't work so well.
Edit: More plays. I'm not sure this plays significantly different game to game. The overall arc seems repetitive. Reducing to 8.2.

item.name: Praga Caput Regni
item.comment:
3 (2) (open)
Nice feel-good game, where you get points for everything. But this point-salady nature also means the game somehow lacks a focus. Also, player interaction is there, but not enough, the amount of blocking is not too great. And it might be a bit too long for what it is.
Still, overall the interesting action selection mechanism, the nice art and components and the feel-good nature of the game make me want to play again.

item.name: Puerto Rico
item.comment:
(open)
Finally played this classic, and I see it's a classic for reason. Very positive impressions after first game at 4p: - Short turns, quick play - A lot of player interaction - with the role choices, "specializing" the ships, race for trading, race for some buildings - Focused scoring - not a point salad with a gazillion unrelated point sources - Good balance between tactical and strategic aspects - Functional components - Well-written rulebook
I like but don't love RFTG, which is a derivative game, but the amount of player interaction makes Puerto Rico much more interesting to me.

item.name: Quacks
item.comment:
4 (3,2) (open)
It has fun moments, but it's extremely random, there is close to zero interaction, and it feels very very light in terms of what decisions you take. And it feels too long for what it is.

item.name: The Quest for El Dorado
item.comment:
(open)
Simple rules, plays quickly, very fun. Has all the good Reiner Knizia properties. Maybe feels a tad over-simplified for my taste, and there is a bit of a runaway leader issue. Still a great game.
From the several Knizia games I've played, I think I like Y&Y, Ra and Blue Lagoon better.

item.name: Ra
item.comment:
(open)
An amazing Reiner Knizia game. Rules are dead simple, turns are short so it plays super breezy, the total game time is not long, but still enough to build some tension. It's been super fun every time we've played it, at 3, 4 or 5 players. Also a very feel-good game, even if you lose, you've had a good time. Production of the 25th Century Games version is great.

item.name: Race for the Galaxy
item.comment:
(open)
It's biggest asset is that it plays very fast (20-40 min per game), and in this time gives sufficient options to build a real engine and exploit it a bit. It's biggest downside is interaction is too low. Yeah, there is some with trying to predict the action selection, but that's about it. Cards lead to variability, but not to a huge extent. Overall it's still a fun game.
For a much more varied experience with a lot higher interaction and more table talk, another card game I highly recommend is Innovation, but it plays slower.
Epic: Upping a tad to 7.5 cause I find I'm often seeking RftG as a quick game with enough level of depth that works well at two. But I still lack more interaction in it.

item.name: Rajas of the Ganges: The Dice Charmers
Ricochet Robots
item.comment:
3-8 (open)
It's a fun activity to do from time to time. Kids enjoy this too. Works well with larger groups too.
But I'd always prefer a "real" strategic game to it.

item.name: Robinson Crusoe: Adventures on the Cursed Island
item.comment:
1-2 (3, maybe 4) (open)
I've found I hate cooperative game, and I'm not a fan of fiddly games, and this ticks both points. I'm also not a solo gamer and this game doesn't benefit from additional players. The randomness with the dice was also meh.
Rules are long and complex, but they do make thematic sense, so play actually flowed well.
Haven't had the desire afterwards to unpack and play again.

item.name: Root
item.comment:
4 (3) (open)
Amazing art and components, as well as world-building. I so much wanted to like this game. But the gameplay felt mechanical and fiddly. I'll definitely give it more chances though, maybe it will grow on me once I play more times with players who are familiar with the game.

item.name: Scythe
item.comment:
4 (5,3) (open)
Amazing art and world-building. But mechanically and in terms of "Wow" moments, it somewhat falls flat. Turns are quick, which is nice. Need to play more, it may grow on me.
Edit: After several games at two players and two games at five players. Neither of these counts works well. It promises waaay more than it delivers. Not enough interactivity. Most times you're not interested in other players' turns almost at all. No "wow" moves. Not enough fun. It feels like a somewhat dull hotchpotch of mechanics in a very shiny pretty wrap.
I played Yellow & Yangtze recently and there are some distant similarities between the two games, but Y&Y is so much more streamlined and there are way more interesting moments.... Reducing rating to 6.9. The art and presentation is great enough to keep me interested in playing a couple more times, but I think I'd be suggesting other games.

item.name: Shackleton Base: A Journey to the Moon
Sidereal Confluence
item.comment:
6, 7, 8, (5, 9, 4) (open)
One partial game only, had to finish after the 4th confluence.
Nice. I don't like realtime games and I was afraid this might have the unpleasant chaotic and stressful feeling of those, but I don't feel this is so much the case here.
The mechanics encourage active participation from everyone. Races are sufficiently different, so understanding strategy would require at least several more plays.
It's a massive table hog. Plays up to 9 people, there's a lot of common stuff, and everyone's personal tableau gets huge too.
Edit: Still, after that first play, I haven't felt the urge to replay this again. Reducing rating.

item.name: Small World
item.comment:
4 (3,5) (open)
It was a very nice game for some time, we played multiple times, then sort of grew tired of it. The heavy setup means we now almost never play it. I still wouldn't turn down a game if someone asks.
Also, there is some amount of kingmaking. A single player who's behind has the power to ruin the game for another player, if they choose so. Generally, other player's decisions can make or break your game without your input and without you having options to interfere, which I am not a big fan of.

item.name: Star Realms: Frontiers
item.comment:
2 (open)
Not a huge fan of deck-building, but at least this one is quick and snappy, so I'd usually be willing to play and would eventually even offer myself, if I have no time or brain-power for something more meaningful.

item.name: Steam
item.comment:
(open)
First play at 3p, liked it a lot. Fast turns, highly interactive, reasonable total time. Nice gameplay ark - the focus and tensions were different throughout the game, and it was getting more and more competitive.
The rulebook is fairly bad. Art and components are also meh. But that does not diminish how good the game itself is.
Have not played AoS and RotW, so cannot compare.

item.name: Summoner Wars (Second Edition)
item.comment:
2 (open)
From a couple of plays - not a bad game, faction abilities are fun, the whole system is clever. But I find that games with direct battling where outcome is directly determined by dice throws are not really for me. Still, I'd probably play a couple more times before trading away.

item.name: Take 5: 30th Anniversary Edition
item.comment:
(open)
Several games on BGA only. Quick and fun, but feels a bit too simple and luck-driven. Would play, but would not seek.
Edit: Some more plays in person, at 8 and 10 players. Confirms impressions the first plays on BGA. One good aspect is that it's a quick game that could play at that number, and even with kids. Overall it's fun, but at least at this count - mostly random. I suppose there would be a tad more depth to it at a lower player count.

item.name: Teotihuacan: City of Gods
item.comment:
4 (3, maybe 2) (open)
Only one play at 3p a long time ago. Haven't had a great desire to table again since, and my son hated it.
Tracks, point salad, efficiency puzzle. Great components and art. Not enough player interaction.
I'm sure there is a deep, strategic game in there if one dedicates the time to it, I'm not sure the whole thing is compelling enough to warrant dedicating that time.

item.name: Terraforming Mars
item.comment:
3 (4,2) (open)
The engine-building is nice here. Downside is that it feels too long for what it is. The player interaction is also not that high, it's mostly multiplayer solitaire. I would have preferred if the map had a bigger impact on the game than it does.
Edit: After some more plays - yes, it's long, but it's fun, raising to 8.

item.name: Through the Ages: A New Story of Civilization
item.comment:
(open)
After two games, not a great fan. Plays very slow, both games took forever without people doing super slow turns, and both times we played the short game, i.e. no age III cards. There seems to be a massive runaway leader issue. Both times a player who, by luck, got a chance to build an early military lead, ended up winning easily. Military advantage snowballs into economic advantage. There is no mechanism for weaker players to stop a runaway leader, even if they collaborate actively. It's a civ game, but there is no sense of real progression - turns go slower and slower with more action points, numbers increase in absolute value, but the core of what players do stays the same. The fact is the whole game you are pushing roughly the same - give or take - blue/yellow cubes up and down. For such a long game, luck of the draw definitely plays a huge role. Interaction is kinda there, to an extent, but extremely negative.
For an actually good civilization game that evokes a sense of change over time, and feels more epic while being 4 times shorter, play Innovation instead, it's infinitely better.
For a tableau/engine builder with more diverse and interesting cards, Terraforming Mars is way better.
Edit: After several days, I do still have an urge to give it another go, upping the rating from 6 to 7.

item.name: Ultimate Railroads
item.comment:
(open)
Single play on BGA, without fully comprehending the rules. Too early to rate, but it did felt a bit too much point-salady, and not sufficiently thematic.

item.name: Undaunted: North Africa
item.comment:
2 (open)
There is luck both in the dice and the card draw. The one coming from the card draw can be mitigated over the course of a game, considering it's a deck builder. But it feels a couple of unlucky dice rolls in a row can predetermine the winner.
Some interesting scenarios, others feel a bit unbalanced, but that may be intentional. I am yet to play through the full campaign.

item.name: Unmatched: Battle of Legends, Volume One
Viscounts of the West Kingdom
item.comment:
(shrink)
One play at 3p. Interesting mechanics, and overall there are fun elements.
But I found it lacking in interaction - at least in our game, everyone focused on their own thing, we specialized in different aspects and there was hardly any reason to check what others are doing or ways to affect their game in a significant way.
Additionally, turns start getting more and more "combotastic", especially around the castle, to an extent it's difficult to plan in which sector of the castle you want to drop your workers, and also turns simply take long till all effects are resolved.
The game also sort-of pushes you in some direction and from there it's easier and more beneficial to just continue in that direction than switch. It becomes an exercise in how effectively you execute tactically cause strategically you take 1-2 decisions early on and then just fly with them.
Despite the negatives, I'd like to give it some more spins, maybe deeper play would open up.
I think for now, after one play each, I'd rank the three games in the trilogy: Architects (played at 5p, fastest, most interactive, most fun moments, quick turns) > Paladins (4p, deeper and allows for strategic play, but less interaction and AP-inducing) > Viscounts (3p).

item.name: War of the Ring: Second Edition
item.comment:
2 (open)
Setup is a total pain. But it's thematic, and usually there's a good buildup during the game until both players are close to winning. We've had games end on a final draw, where either player could have won depending on which tile was drawn.
Rules are complex, but tie well with the theme and make enough sense, that actually once you understand them and start playing, it's not hard to follow them correctly, there aren't that many exceptions.
But with the complex setup, hundreds of pieces, and fiddly rules that require some refreshing every time we open the game, and the fact it's a table hog that we may have to play over several consecutive evenings (so we play it on the floor), the result is we play it only 1-2 times per year.

item.name: The White Castle
item.comment:
(open)
One play. Not bad, but not great either. Components and art are nice, small package is great, and does pack a "bigger" game than one would expect.
In theory, the game should achieve a lot with only 9 turns "simple" actions.
In practice, a lot of the turns are long and tiresome, mostly backtracking "I want to do this, but to use it effectively, I would need that, so let me see how to chain things efficiently", trying to find which of many possible variants give you the necessary resources for the full combo. Combos feel nice when you pull them, but I don't think they are worth the long downtime.
As a result interaction is too little, players are mostly heads down, the majority of the talk is really cooperatively puzzling out how a player can achieve what they want, helping them so they can find their turn faster, or simply explaining what you do so others can make sure you're not making mistakes (as it's easy to make them).
Maybe it gets better with experience, and I'll give it some more shots to feel whether the variable setup would result in actually variable games, but I'm not convinced there is enough interesting things here to warrant too many plays.

item.name: Wingspan
item.comment:
3 (4,2) (open)
Fairly light tableau builder. Way overhyped, IMHO, due to excellent production, art and component quality. Too much multiplayer solitaire for my taste - there are cards that interact with other player's turns, but the level of interaction is too low. Cards are too random to even passively block other players. There is a high amount of randomness in both card draws and dice.
For a tableau builder with cards that interact with one another in interesting ways, which plays in roughly the same time, and feels much meatier, I vastly recommend Innovation over Wingspan.

item.name: Yellow & Yangtze
item.comment:
(open)
Growing on me and turning into one of my favorite games. Not much that there isn't to like here. Classic Knizia - simple rules, deep play.
- Clean and simple rules, make thematic sense, easy to recall and teach. - Very fast setup and tear-down. - Quick turns. - Very interactive, you are invested in every player's actions. - Interesting game arc, dramatic moves - Strategies are varied and non-obvious. - Nice artwork and nice components.
Plays best with four, but three is good too. Haven't tried it at two.

item.name: Zoo Vadis
item.comment:
Great quick trading/negotiation game. Simple rules. Great components and presentation. Fun, engaging gameplay. 8.5.
Edit: Reducing to 7.5 after more plays. Negotiations on a player's turn could sometimes drag a bit, leading to games that last longer than it's ok for a game of this depth.
